1	# ADR 0048 — Per-period metrics, yearly seasonality and seasonal periods on the anomaly monitor
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted (2026-10-13)
4	- **Date:** 2026-10-13
5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
6	- **Related:** ADR [0012](0012-monitor-kind-seam.md) (monitor kinds, `metric_value`), [0016](0016-severity-derivation-semantics.md) (severity bands), [0041](0041-history-audit-strategy.md) (audit), [0047](0047-automated-coverage-loop.md) (automatic baselines, which this does not extend).
7	
8	## Context
9	
10	The anomaly monitor is the one place in DataQ with a learned baseline: every other monitor
11	kind (freshness, volume, aggregate, schema drift) compares against a fixed threshold or the
12	previous run. It scores a run against the check's own recent history: the last `window` runs,
13	or the last `window` runs on the same weekday. It keeps `window` observations, seven times
14	that with weekday seasonality: weeks or months of history, never years. And it watches three
15	things, all whole-table: the row count, the age of the newest timestamp, and the column
16	profile.
17	
18	That is the wrong shape for data with a yearly rhythm. A sales table has sale periods. Its
19	whole-table row count only grows, so it says nothing about them. And if DataQ watched sales
20	per day instead, the last few weeks would be the wrong comparison twice over: every recurring
21	peak would look like an anomaly, and a peak that should have arrived and did not (a load that
22	failed during the sale) would look normal.
23	
24	Two things are missing: a metric that is a value *per period*, and a baseline that knows what
25	this time of year usually looks like.
26	
27	## Decision
28	
29	1. **Two per-period metrics on the anomaly kind.** `period_row_count` counts the rows whose
30	   date falls in a period; `period_sum` sums a numeric column over them. The check names a
31	   `date_column`, a `period` (`day` or `week`) and, for the sum, a `value_column`.
32	
33	   - **Buckets** are calendar dates of the column as the warehouse returns it (the column
34	     cast to a date). A column with no time zone is taken at face value. A zone-aware
35	     timestamp is bucketed in the warehouse session's zone, which DataQ does not set; the
36	     editor says so.
37	   - **Which periods are complete** is decided in the check's `timezone` (an IANA name,
38	     default UTC), and a period is judged only once it has been closed for `settle_hours`
39	     (default 6), so a suite scheduled just after midnight does not judge yesterday before
40	     the nightly load has landed.
41	   - **One point per period, written once.** The verdict is about the most recent settled
42	     period. A second run before the next period settles measures it again for the result
43	     but does not add or change a stored point. Rows that arrive after a period was judged
44	     are not reflected in its point; that is the price of a point meaning "what the table
45	     held when DataQ judged it".
46	
47	   These are authored checks on SQL datasources.
48	
49	2. **History is seeded once, then accumulated.** On the run that finds no baseline, one
50	   grouped query reads up to three years of periods from the table's own rows. Every period
51	   before the one being judged is stored marked `backfilled`; the judged one, and every one
52	   after it, is `observed`. The mark never changes. The two are kept apart because they are
53	   different evidence: an observed point is what the table held when DataQ looked, and a
54	   backfilled point is what the table says today about the past, which a restatement or a
55	   purge can have changed. Each result reports how many of the points it was scored against
56	   were backfilled.
57	
58	   Seeding is one scan of the table. It can be switched off on the check (`backfill: false`)
59	   for a warehouse that bills per query or a table whose old rows are archived; the check then
60	   starts empty and waits. Dropping a check's baseline seeds it again.
61	
62	3. **Yearly seasonality is a seasonal index over the rolling baseline.** With `yearly: true`:
63	
64	   - The *level* at a period is the median of the `window` periods before it.
65	   - The *index* for a period is what the matching period in an earlier year was, divided by
66	     the level then. With more than one earlier year the index is their median.
67	   - *Matching.* A day is matched to the same weekday nearest the same calendar date in the
68	     earlier year (52 weeks back, then 104, and so on, corrected to the nearest such
69	     weekday); a week to the week containing that date. There is no "week 53" case. A peak
70	     tied to a fixed date (25 December) or to a moving one (a sale) does not line up this
71	     way, and needs a declared period (decision 4).
72	   - *Scoring.* The expected value is the level now times the index. The run is scored on
73	     how far it is from that **in proportion to it**, against how far each prior period was
74	     from what was expected of it. A sale that ran at 2.4 times its surrounding weeks last
75	     year is expected at 2.4 times now, so arriving near 2.4 times is normal and arriving
76	     flat is not; and a sale day five times an ordinary day has five times the room.
77	
78	     > **Amended 2026-10-14.** As first written the distance was taken in the metric's own
79	     > units, so a peak had only an ordinary day's room and a sale that repeated within the
80	     > range of earlier years still alerted. It is proportional now. With two or more
81	     > earlier years, how much they disagreed about the size of the peak is added to the
82	     > spread, and the result shows each year's ratio: two years with a sale and one without
83	     > make a loose comparison, and the check says so instead of pretending to precision.
84	     > Where the expected value is zero (the shop was closed that day last year) there is no
85	     > proportion to take, and the distance is taken as it stands.
86	
87	   - *When it does not apply.* The index is used only where it means something: the level
88	     then was above zero and neither it nor the matched value is negative. Otherwise, and
89	     for a period with no earlier year to match, the index is 1, which is exactly today's
90	     behaviour, and the result says the yearly comparison was not applied and why (no
91	     earlier year, a zero level, a negative sum).
92	
93	   Every number in that chain is in the result: the level, the index, the years it came from
94	   and the expected value. Nothing is skipped for want of a year: the check is useful from
95	   the day it has `min_points`, and becomes seasonal when the history allows.
96	
97	4. **Yearly seasonality is a property of the anomaly kind, not of one metric.** It is
98	   offered on every metric that is one number per run: the two per-period metrics, the
99	   whole-table row count and the freshness age. For the whole-table metrics a "period" is a
100	   calendar day, the stored point for a day is the last run's value that day, and history
101	   can only accumulate: there is nothing to seed a past row count from. Weekday seasonality
102	   stays as it is and combines with it. The column profile does not get it: it is hundreds
103	   of series per check, and three years of each is not a baseline, it is a warehouse.
104	
105	   > **Amended 2026-10-14.** The first build tried "one stored point a day, the day's last
106	   > run" for the whole-table metrics, and it was wrong: a check that runs hourly was scored
107	   > against the previous days' last readings (a freshness age of one hour against priors of
108	   > twenty-one), and switching the setting on or off threw history away. A whole-table
109	   > metric needs its run-by-run points kept as they are, with a separate one-a-day series
110	   > for the yearly index beside them. That is its own phase; until it ships, `yearly` is
111	   > accepted on the per-period metrics only.
112	
113	   Automatic coverage (ADR 0047) gets it through the setting it already has: the baseline
114	   shape gains a `yearly` switch, default off, which applies to the automatic row-count and
115	   freshness baselines. The per-period metrics are **not** added to automatic coverage: an
116	   automatic baseline assumes nothing about a table, and choosing which column is the
117	   business date and which is the amount is a claim a person makes. Automatic coverage may
118	   later *suggest* one for review.
119	
120	5. **Seasonal periods are declared by people and detected from history. Only declared ones
121	   change a verdict.**
122	
123	   - **Declared.** A workspace calendar of named periods, each either recurring (a month and
124	     day range, every year) or dated (explicit start and end, for a sale that moves). Admins
125	     manage it; changes are audited. It is workspace-wide because a sale period is a fact
126	     about the business. A check names the calendar entries that apply to it, and none do by
127	     default, so adding an entry changes no check until someone attaches it.
128	   - **What a declared period does.** A day inside it is matched to the same offset within
129	     that period's previous occurrence, which is what makes a moving sale or a fixed date
130	     line up. Periods inside it are left out of the level, so the weeks after a sale are not
131	     judged against the sale. And when the period has no earlier occurrence in the history,
132	     the check is told a rise is expected and cannot say how large: a value **above** what
133	     the rolling baseline expects is reported as within the declared period and not banded,
134	     while a value **below** it is judged as usual. A load that fails during a first-year
135	     sale still alerts.
136	   > **Amended 2026-10-19 (phase 4).** Three decisions the build had to make. (1) *A dated
137	   > entry's previous occurrence.* A dated entry is one-off by itself; the schema makes
138	   > "occurrences of one period" explicit with a `series` on dated entries, matched
139	   > case-insensitively, and a check attaches each year's entry it wants compared. A dated
140	   > entry with no earlier entry of its series among the check's attachments is a first
141	   > year. (2) *29 February.* A recurring bound may be 29 February; in a year without one it
142	   > is 28 February. The same offset into a previous occurrence that was shorter (a leap-year
143	   > sale that ran a day longer) has no match in that occurrence and the next earlier one is
144	   > tried. (3) *Attachments live in the check's config* (`seasonal_periods`, a list of ids)
145	   > rather than a join table, because every surface that carries a check's definition —
146	   > `check_versions`, export/import, apply, the audit snapshot and a dry run that has no
147	   > check row — is config-shaped. Deleting an entry a check still names is refused by the
148	   > service, naming the checks, under a row lock the attaching save shares. A calendar
149	   > entry applies only with `yearly` on, since lining a day up with an earlier occurrence
150	   > is the yearly comparison; attaching one without it is refused rather than ignored.
151	   > Each result on an attached check reports what it would have scored with no calendar.
152	
153	   - **Detected.** Read from a check's own history when someone asks: a run of periods at or
154	     above 1.5 times the level. Seen at the same time in two or more years it is *recurring*;
155	     in one year, *seen once*. Detected periods are shown on the check's trend so a person
156	     can see why a verdict came out as it did, and an admin can promote one to the calendar.
157	     Until then a detected period is a description: it is not stored and it changes no
158	     score. The seasonal index already carries a recurring peak into the expected value
159	     without it.
160	   > **Amended 2026-10-20 (phase 5).** The thresholds and the promote flow, as built. (1) *The
161	   > level* is taken as scoring takes it, over the same `window` periods before (by weekday
162	   > with `seasonality`, attached declared periods left out): their median with `yearly`
163	   > on, their mean without, since that is what a check without `yearly` is scored against; a period is looked at only once
164	   > `min_points` periods precede it. A peak outlasting about half the window's prior
165	   > periods (same-weekday ones with `seasonality`) lifts that median with it, so its tail is not detected; an attached entry covering it is what fixes
166	   > that, as it does for scoring. (2) *A run* is consecutive qualifying periods: at least
167	   > two days, since one day is a spike rather than a period, or one week. A day with no
168	   > point ends a run; no gap is bridged. (3) *The same time* in two years means the runs,
169	   > laid on one year, come within seven days of each other, so a sale that moves by up to a
170	   > week still matches. Two runs in one season (a sale split by an ordinary day, or one that
171	   > crosses the new year) are one year, not two. (4) *What is returned*: each period's
172	   > occurrences per year with their peak ratio and how many of their points were backfilled,
173	   > the month/day span a recurring one covers, the attached entries that overlap it, and how
174	   > much history stood behind the answer; when there was nothing to look at, the reason (not
175	   > a per-period metric, no history, too little history). It is computed on request from the
176	   > stored points, a separate read from the trend's baseline read so the trend view asks for
177	   > it only on a per-period check. (5) *Promoting* is an admin action that re-reads the
178	   > history and names the period by the start of its most recent occurrence, so a period the
179	   > history no longer shows is refused rather than invented, and one an existing entry
180	   > already covers is refused naming that entry, so a season is declared once. A recurring period becomes a
181	   > recurring entry over that span, one seen once a dated entry. Attaching it to the check is
182	   > optional and done in the same transaction, so a check that cannot take it (no `yearly`)
183	   > leaves no entry behind. The entry is audited as created, with what it was promoted from.
184	
185	6. **Retention.** A check with `yearly` on, or on a per-period metric, keeps three years of
186	   periods plus its window (about 1,100 daily points). Other anomaly checks keep what they
187	   keep today.
188	
189	## Phases
190	
191	1. Per-period metrics: measurement, validation, one point per settled period.
192	2. Seeding from the table and three-year retention.
193	3. Yearly seasonality in scoring, for the per-period metrics.
194	4. The declared calendar (schema first, on its own), and attaching entries to a check.
195	5. Detected periods and the read surfaces (REST, MCP).
196	6. Check editor, trend view and calendar UI; user docs.
197	7. Yearly seasonality for the whole-table metrics (a one-a-day series beside the run-by-run
198	   points), then the `yearly` switch in the automatic-coverage baseline shape, with an
199	   amendment to ADR 0047.
200	
201	## Consequences
202	
203	- A recurring peak stops paging people, and a missing one starts to.
204	- The first yearly verdict needs a year of history. Seeding supplies it for a per-period
205	  metric where the table still holds its past. Everywhere else the check waits a year, and
206	  says so on every result until then.
207	- One earlier year cannot tell a recurring sale from a one-off. The index uses it anyway,
208	  because one year is better than none, and the result names how many years stand behind it.
209	- A backfilled baseline trusts the table's history. Marking the points is what keeps that
210	  visible.
211	- Three years of daily points is a larger baseline row than any check has had. It is one JSONB
212	  value per check and is read once per run. Switching `yearly` on for automatic coverage
213	  multiplies that by every covered table, which is why it is off by default there.
214	- Late rows do not revise a judged period. A table that fills in slowly needs a longer
215	  `settle_hours`, not a re-read.
216	
217	## Considered and rejected
218	
219	- **A report of when the sales are**, for analysts to plan from: that is business analysis,
220	  and a BI tool is the place for it. DataQ shows the periods it detected because they explain
221	  its verdicts, not as a product of their own.
222	- **Accumulating only:** no yearly verdict for a year, and two before a period can be called
223	  recurring, on tables that already hold the history.
224	- **Backfilling only:** nothing would record what the table held when each run looked, so a
225	  later restatement would silently rewrite the baseline.
226	- **Re-reading recent periods on every run** to pick up late rows: it rewrites observed
227	  points after they were judged, which is the same objection.
228	- **Yearly seasonality on the per-period metrics alone:** a snapshot table that is replaced
229	  every night has a row count with seasons too, and the automatic baselines would never get
230	  it.
231	- **Comparing only against the same period in earlier years:** two or three points give no
232	  spread to score against. The index keeps the recent window as the source of spread.
233	- **Matching by ISO week number:** some years have a week 53 and the earlier year does not.
234	- **Skipping every verdict inside a declared period with no history:** it would hide a failed
235	  load during a sale, which is the incident this exists to catch.
236	- **Letting a detected period change the baseline before a person confirms it:** an
237	  unreviewed guess would move verdicts with nothing in the result to say so.
238	- **A calendar entry that applies to every check automatically:** one admin entry would
239	  change the verdicts of checks on tables the sale never touches.
240	- **A forecasting library** (seasonal decomposition or similar): a new dependency whose
241	  verdict cannot be explained from the numbers in the result.
242	- **Declared periods typed into each check:** the same sale would be entered again for every
243	  table it touches. A check attaches entries; it does not define them.
244

"""The declared seasonal calendar (ADR 0048 decision 5): read by anyone signed in, so a check
author can attach entries; changed by workspace admins only."""

from __future__ import annotations

import uuid
from datetime import date, datetime
from typing import Annotated, Any, Literal

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, status
from pydantic import Field
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

from backend.app.api.v1._base import ApiModel, ApiRequestModel
from backend.app.core.auth import AdminUser, get_current_user
from backend.app.db.models import SeasonalPeriod
from backend.app.db.session import get_db
from backend.app.services import seasonal_detection_service
from backend.app.services import seasonal_period_service as svc
from backend.app.services.suite_authz import require_permission

router = APIRouter(
    prefix="/admin/seasonal-periods",
    tags=["admin"],
    dependencies=[Depends(get_current_user)],
)

Kind = Literal["recurring", "dated"]


class SeasonalPeriodWrite(ApiRequestModel):
    """A recurring entry sets the four month/day fields (the range may wrap the year end:
    20 December to 5 January; 29 February is taken as 28 February in other years). A dated
    entry sets `start_date` and `end_date`, and optionally a `series`: dated entries sharing
    a series are occurrences of one period across years, which is how a moving sale finds
    its previous occurrence."""

    name: str = Field(max_length=svc.NAME_MAX)
    kind: Kind
    start_month: int | None = None
    start_day: int | None = None
    end_month: int | None = None
    end_day: int | None = None
    start_date: date | None = None
    end_date: date | None = None
    series: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.SERIES_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.NOTE_MAX)


class SeasonalPeriodPatch(ApiRequestModel):
    """Any field left out keeps its value; the result is validated whole, so a kind change
    must send the new kind's fields."""

    name: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.NAME_MAX)
    kind: Kind | None = None
    start_month: int | None = None
    start_day: int | None = None
    end_month: int | None = None
    end_day: int | None = None
    start_date: date | None = None
    end_date: date | None = None
    series: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.SERIES_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.NOTE_MAX)


class SeasonalPeriodRead(ApiModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    name: str
    kind: Kind
    start_month: int | None
    start_day: int | None
    end_month: int | None
    end_day: int | None
    start_date: date | None
    end_date: date | None
    series: str | None
    note: str | None
    #: Checks whose config names this entry. Deleting is refused while it is above zero.
    attached_checks: int
    created_at: datetime
    updated_at: datetime

    @classmethod
    def from_model(cls, row: SeasonalPeriod, attached: int) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
        return cls(
            id=row.id,
            **svc.fields_of(row),
            attached_checks=attached,
            created_at=row.created_at,
            updated_at=row.updated_at,
        )


def _read(db: Session, row: SeasonalPeriod) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
    return SeasonalPeriodRead.from_model(row, len(svc.attached_checks(db, row.id)))


@router.get("", response_model=list[SeasonalPeriodRead], summary="List the seasonal calendar")
def list_seasonal_periods(db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)]) -> list[SeasonalPeriodRead]:
    counts = svc.attached_counts(db)
    return [SeasonalPeriodRead.from_model(r, counts.get(r.id, 0)) for r in svc.list_periods(db)]


@router.get("/{period_id}", response_model=SeasonalPeriodRead, summary="Read one entry")
def get_seasonal_period(
    period_id: uuid.UUID, db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)]
) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
    return _read(db, svc.get_period(db, period_id))


@router.post(
    "",
    response_model=SeasonalPeriodRead,
    status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
    summary="Add a calendar entry (admin)",
)
def create_seasonal_period(
    payload: SeasonalPeriodWrite,
    current_user: AdminUser,
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
    row = svc.create_period(db, payload.model_dump(), actor_id=current_user.id)
    return _read(db, row)


class SeasonalPeriodPromote(ApiRequestModel):
    """Promote a period detected in a check's history
    (`GET /suites/{suite_id}/checks/{check_id}/seasonal-periods/detected`) to the calendar.
    `start` is the detected period's `start` (its most recent season); the server reads the
    history again and refuses a start it no longer shows (404), or a season an entry on the
    calendar already covers (409, naming the entry to attach instead). A recurring period becomes a
    month/day range, a period seen once a dated entry (`series` applies only to that).
    `attach` also attaches the new entry to the check, which needs `yearly` on it."""

    suite_id: uuid.UUID
    check_id: uuid.UUID
    start: date
    name: str = Field(max_length=svc.NAME_MAX)
    series: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.SERIES_MAX)
    note: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=svc.NOTE_MAX)
    attach: bool = False


@router.post(
    "/promote",
    response_model=SeasonalPeriodRead,
    status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
    summary="Add a detected period to the calendar (admin)",
)
def promote_detected_period(
    payload: SeasonalPeriodPromote,
    current_user: AdminUser,
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
    require_permission(
        db, payload.suite_id, current_user.id, minimum="edit" if payload.attach else "view"
    )
    row = seasonal_detection_service.promote(
        db,
        suite_id=payload.suite_id,
        check_id=payload.check_id,
        start=payload.start,
        fields=payload.model_dump(include={"name", "series", "note"}),
        attach=payload.attach,
        actor_id=current_user.id,
    )
    return _read(db, row)


@router.patch("/{period_id}", response_model=SeasonalPeriodRead, summary="Edit an entry (admin)")
def update_seasonal_period(
    period_id: uuid.UUID,
    payload: SeasonalPeriodPatch,
    current_user: AdminUser,
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> SeasonalPeriodRead:
    fields: dict[str, Any] = payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    row = svc.update_period(db, period_id, fields, actor_id=current_user.id)
    return _read(db, row)


@router.delete(
    "/{period_id}",
    status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT,
    summary="Delete an entry (admin; refused while any check names it)",
)
def delete_seasonal_period(
    period_id: uuid.UUID,
    current_user: AdminUser,
    db: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_db)],
) -> None:
    svc.delete_period(db, period_id, actor_id=current_user.id)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeclaredEffect:
    """What a declared period did to one run's score."""

    entry: DeclaredPeriod
    occurrence: Occurrence
    offset_days: int
    #: The matching days in earlier occurrences the index came from.
    matched: tuple[date, ...] = ()
    #: No earlier occurrence in the history: a rise is expected and its size unknown.
    first_year: bool = False
    #: False when the first-year rule withheld the band (the value was above the level).
    banded: bool = True

    def as_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "entry_id": str(self.entry.id),
            "name": self.entry.name,
            "kind": self.entry.kind,
            "occurrence": {
                "start": self.occurrence.start.isoformat(),
                "end": self.occurrence.end.isoformat(),
            },
            "offset_days": self.offset_days,
            "matched": [d.isoformat() for d in self.matched],
            "first_year": self.first_year,
            "banded": self.banded,
        }


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class YearlyScore:
    """A run scored with the yearly comparison, or the reason it was scored without."""

    applied: bool
    reason: str | None = None
    level: float | None = None
    index: float | None = None
    #: The earlier periods the index came from, newest first, and what each was against its
    #: own level then. Years that disagree widen the spread; the result shows them.
    matched: tuple[date, ...] = ()
    ratios: tuple[float, ...] = ()
    #: The level times the index: what this time of year is expected to be.
    expected: float | None = None
    z_score: float | None = None
    #: The centre and spread the run was scored against, in the metric's own units, so that
    #: ``|value - centre| / spread`` is the z-score.
    centre: float | None = None
    spread: float | None = None
    degenerate: bool = False
    #: Set when the run's day is inside a declared period.
    declared: DeclaredEffect | None = None
    #: Earlier points left out of the level for falling inside a declared period.
    excluded_from_level: int = 0

    @property
    def banded(self) -> bool:
        return self.declared is None or self.declared.banded

    def as_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        if not self.applied:
            return {"applied": False, "reason": self.reason}
        return {
            "applied": True,
            "level": _rounded(self.level),
            "index": _rounded(self.index),
            "expected": _rounded(self.expected),
            "matched": [d.isoformat() for d in self.matched],
            "ratios": [round(r, 4) for r in self.ratios],
            "years": len(self.matched),
        }


def _rounded(value: float | None) -> float | None:
    return None if value is None else round(value, 6)

def observation_time(
    params: AnomalyParams, now: datetime, settled: tuple[date, date] | None = None
) -> tuple[datetime, dict[str, Any]]:
    """When this run's point is dated, and the period fields its result carries. A per-period
    point is dated at the start of its period (a calendar label, stored as midnight UTC)."""
    spec = params.period
    if spec is None:
        return now, {}
    start, end = settled or spec.settled(now)
    return datetime.combine(start, time.min, tzinfo=UTC), {
        "period": {
            "start": start.isoformat(),
            "end": end.isoformat(),
            "unit": spec.unit,
            "timezone": spec.timezone,
            "settle_hours": spec.settle_hours,
        }
    }


def trim(observations: list[Observation], params: AnomalyParams) -> list[Observation]:
    """Keep only the most recent `retained_observations` (chronological order in)."""
    retained = params.retained_observations
    return observations[-retained:] if retained else []


# ───────────────────────── scoring (pure) ─────────────────────────


def _considered(
    observations: list[Observation], now: datetime, params: AnomalyParams
) -> list[Observation]:
    """The prior points this run is scored against, newest-last."""
    considered = (
        [o for o in observations if o.ts.weekday() == now.weekday()]
        if params.seasonality
        else list(observations)
    )


def declared_payload(
    check: Check,
    compared: seasonal.YearlyScore,
    *,
    without: seasonal.YearlyScore,
    ordinary_z: float | None,
    calendar: seasonal.Calendar,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """``observed_value.declared``: which entry the judged period fell in and how it was
    matched, how many earlier points the calendar kept out of the level, and the z-score and
    tier the run would have had with no calendar attached."""
    z_without = without.z_score if without.applied else ordinary_z
    z_with = compared.z_score if compared.applied and compared.banded else None
    with_status = _banded(check, z_with) if compared.applied else _banded(check, ordinary_z)
    without_status = _banded(check, z_without)
    return {
        "attached": [str(e.id) for e in calendar.entries],
        "missing": [str(i) for i in calendar.missing],
        "inside": compared.declared.as_dict() if compared.declared is not None else None,
        "excluded_from_level": compared.excluded_from_level,
        "z_score_without": None if z_without is None else round(z_without, 6),
        "verdict_without": without_status,
        "verdict_changed": with_status != without_status,
    }


# ───────────────────────── run executor ─────────────────────────


def build_anomaly_executor(
    session: Session,
    *,
    connection: Connection,
    target_table: str,
    target_schema: str | None,
    target_catalog: str | None,
    secret_store: SecretStore,

        # The three-year scan runs BEFORE the row is locked: holding the lock across it would
        # make a concurrent run of this check time out waiting. Decided on an unlocked read;
        # the locked read below settles who keeps what.
        attempt = None
        if persist and settled is not None:
            seen = stored_seed(get_baseline(session, check.id), params)
            if seeding_due(params, seen):
                attempt = _seed(check, params, settled[0], seen)
        # Read-modify-write: the observation list this run appends to must not be read by a
        # concurrent run of the same check, or one measurement is silently lost.
        row = get_baseline(session, check.id, for_update=persist)
        observations = load_observations(row, params)
        seed = stored_seed(row, params)
        seeded_now = attempt is not None and seeding_due(params, seed)
        if attempt is not None and seeded_now:
            # Still wanted now the row is ours (a concurrent run may have seeded meanwhile).
            # Periods a run already judged keep their observed point.
            held = {o.ts for o in observations}
            added = [o for o in attempt.points if o.ts not in held and o.ts < at]
            observations = sorted([*observations, *added], key=lambda o: o.ts)
            seed = dict(attempt.report)
            if seed["status"] == "done":
                seed["points"] = len(added)  # what was kept, not what the scan returned
        elif params.period is not None and seed is None and persist:
            seed = {"status": "off"}  # backfill is switched off and has never run
        # A per-period metric is about a period, not about when the run happened: its point
        # is stamped with the period, scored against earlier periods only, and written once.
        dated = params.period is not None
        earlier = [o for o in observations if o.ts < at] if dated else observations
        already_recorded = params.period is not None and any(o.ts == at for o in observations)
        considered = _considered(earlier, at, params)
        payload = {
            **build_score_payload(value, [o.value for o in considered], params),
            **period_fields,

        if params.yearly:

            calendar = (
                seasonal_period_service.calendar_for(session, params.seasonal_periods)
                if params.seasonal_periods
                else None
            )
            compared = seasonal.History(by_day, params, calendar).score(at.date(), value)
            payload["yearly"] = compared.as_dict()
            if calendar is not None:
                # What the calendar did to this run, beside what the run would have scored
                # without it, so a reader can tell when the calendar changed the verdict.
                payload["declared"] = declared_payload(
                    check,
                    compared,
                    without=seasonal.History(by_day, params).score(at.date(), value),
                    ordinary_z=payload.get("z_score"),
                    calendar=calendar,
                )

                # A first-year declared period: a rise was expected and its size unknown.
                payload["within_declared_period"] = True
                payload["reason"] = "within_declared_period"
            if compared.applied and compared.centre is not None:
                # `mean` and `stddev` are what the run was scored against, in the metric's
                # own units, so `|value - mean| / stddev` is the z-score for any reader.
                payload.update(

                        "mean": round(compared.centre, 6),
                        "stddev": round(compared.spread or 0.0, 6),
                        "deviation": round(value - compared.centre, 6),

            # `captured_at` is when learning STARTED (the row's first capture — no `onupdate`,

            payload["baseline_captured_at"] = row.captured_at.isoformat()
            payload["baseline_updated_at"] = row.updated_at.isoformat()

content.content:
# Browser E2E (Playwright)

Drives the **real app in a browser** under dev-bypass auth against the seeded
demo dataset — the other half of the full-stack smoke (#128). The httpx API
smoke (`backend/scripts/e2e_smoke.py`) proves `HTTP → service → DB`; this proves
the React UI a user actually clicks: `browser → Vite proxy → api → DB`.

> Live `test()`/runs against real Snowflake/S3/etc. stay out of scope (no creds
> locally — the documented deferred smoke). The connectivity tests here
> **fail-soft**; the specs assert the health/error path renders, not that a real
> datasource is reachable.

## Specs

| Spec                          | Covers                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `smoke.spec.ts`               | dev-bypass auth, app shell, sider nav                                                                                   |
| `connections.spec.ts`         | seeded connections grouped by type, "Test all" health path                                                              |
| `suites.spec.ts`              | seeded suite → checks; check + suite authoring round-trips                                                              |
| `datasource-browse.spec.ts`   | run-target browse pickers (UC catalog → schema → table, S3 folder → file); listings answered by `page.route`            |
| `results.spec.ts`             | seeded runs, run-detail drill-down, pipeline-runs feed                                                                  |
| `schedules.spec.ts`           | SchedulesPanel: add / pause / delete + invalid-cron 422 path                                                            |
| `trigger-bindings.spec.ts`    | TriggersPanel: bind pipeline / disable / remove (seeded ADF connection)                                                 |
| `notifications.spec.ts`       | NotificationsPanel: threshold routing persisted across reload; write-only webhook affordance                            |
| `a11y.spec.ts`                | axe-core (`@axe-core/playwright`) scan of every route in both themes, ratcheted against a baseline — see below          |
| `keyboard.spec.ts`            | keyboard-only traversal in a real browser: skip link, focus follows navigation, runs/assets/suites open without a mouse |
| `dashboard.spec.ts`           | Dashboard KPI cards, trend / per-suite / recent runs with seeded data, the get-started first-run path                   |
| `check-editor.spec.ts`        | check-editor variants: freshness / volume / anomaly monitors, Monaco custom SQL, comparison                             |
| `assets.spec.ts`              | Assets tree drill-down, the "All assets" table lens, health across ≥2 suites on a shared asset                          |
| `lineage-graph.spec.ts`       | lineage graph on an asset (depth ≥2 both ways, clickable nodes) + its mobile scroll containment                         |
| `admin.spec.ts`               | admin pages: overview health signals, deep links, integrations, compliance/audit chain, DSR, member roles + admission   |
| `roles.spec.ts`               | per-role perspectives (ADR 0033): admin / member / viewer, using the PATs `seed_dev` mints                              |
| `mobile-nav.spec.ts`          | 390px overlay nav: drawer instead of an inline sider, scrim closes without navigating                                   |
| `share-drawer-mobile.spec.ts` | share drawer at 390px stays on-screen                                                                                   |

## Accessibility floor (#1670)

`a11y.spec.ts` runs axe-core over **every route** — the list pages, the six admin sub-pages,
profile, 404, and the id-addressed authoring/detail routes (ids resolved through the API) — once
per theme. Dark surfaces are keyed `route:/…@dark`, and each scan asserts `data-theme` first, so a
dark scan that silently rendered light cannot pass. Add a route to `App.tsx` and it belongs here
too. (The sign-in screen has no dev-bypass equivalent — `e2e-otp/a11y.spec.ts` covers it; its card
is white in both themes.) Each scan waits for the page to finish loading (`scripts/a11y/settle.ts`)
— a scan that lands mid-load sees fewer violations and the ratchet cannot tell. Only
`serious`/`critical` violations are kept. It **ratchets** against the committed
`frontend/a11y-baseline.json` (shared with the Vitest component lane in
`tests/a11y/components.a11y.test.tsx` via `frontend/scripts/a11y/ratchet.ts`) rather than requiring
every existing violation fixed first — a run fails only on a violation NOT already in the baseline.

Regenerate it deliberately (never by hand-editing the JSON) with `pnpm a11y:baseline` — it needs
the same stack this lane already needs (below), plus the OTP stack for the sign-in half; explain
the diff in your PR when you do.

antd Select gotchas (learned per spec, reuse these): rc-select pre-highlights
option 0 when nothing is selected, so `Enter` alone takes the first option and
`ArrowDown`+`Enter` takes the **second**; option nodes live in an off-viewport
rc-virtual-list measurement container, so `getByRole('option').click()` is
flaky — prefer keyboard navigation with the arrow-delta computed from the
currently rendered value (see `notifications.spec.ts`).

## Run it locally

1. Bring up the stack and seed the demo data:

   ```bash
   # dev-bypass is a contributor opt-in — see CONTRIBUTING.md "Developer bypass"
   docker compose up -d            # postgres + redis + openbao + api + worker + beat + frontend
   conda run -n dataq python -m backend.scripts.seed_dev
   ```

2. Install browsers once, then run:

   ```bash
   cd frontend
   pnpm install
   pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
   pnpm e2e            # headless
   pnpm e2e:ui         # Playwright UI mode (watch/debug)
   ```

def _run_with_result(
    db_session: Any,
    suite_id: str,
    check_id: str,
    *,
    status: str,
    metric_value: float | None,
    age_days: float,
) -> None:
    when = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=age_days)
    run = Run(suite_id=uuid.UUID(suite_id), status="succeeded", created_at=when)
    db_session.add(run)
    db_session.flush()
    db_session.add(
        Result(
            run_id=run.id,
            check_id=uuid.UUID(check_id),
            status=status,
            metric_value=metric_value,
            created_at=when,
        )
    )
    db_session.commit()


def test_history_returns_results_oldest_first(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    sid = _suite_id(client, db_session)
    cid = client.post(f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/checks", json=_payload()).json()["id"]
    _run_with_result(db_session, sid, cid, status="pass", metric_value=0.0, age_days=2)
    _run_with_result(db_session, sid, cid, status="warn", metric_value=2.5, age_days=0)

    history = client.get(f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/checks/{cid}/history").json()
    assert [p["status"] for p in history] == ["pass", "warn"]  # chronological
    assert [p["metric_value"] for p in history] == [0.0, 2.5]


def test_history_empty_for_check_with_no_runs(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    sid = _suite_id(client, db_session)

    assert resp.json() == []


def test_history_honours_limit_keeping_most_recent(client: TestClient, db_session: Any) -> None:
    sid = _suite_id(client, db_session)
    cid = client.post(f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/checks", json=_payload()).json()["id"]
    for age in (3, 2, 1):
        _run_with_result(db_session, sid, cid, status="pass", metric_value=age, age_days=age)

    history = client.get(f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/checks/{cid}/history?limit=2").json()
    # Latest 2 by run time, returned chronologically: age=2 then age=1.
    assert [p["metric_value"] for p in history] == [2.0, 1.0]
    resp = client.get(f"/api/v1/suites/{sid}/checks/{cid}/history?limit=0")
    assert resp.status_code == 422

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Scratch stack for the docs screenshot/video lane (frontend/e2e-docs/).
# Mirrors CI's frontend-e2e job — dev-bypass auth, seeded demo data — on its
# own database, OpenBao KV mount and ports, so the developer's compose stack
# (and its orphan-secret sweep) never sees it. Reuses the compose Postgres
# (:5432), Redis (:6379, db 3) and OpenBao (:8200).
#
#   scripts/docs/capture-stack.sh start    # migrate + seed + api :8001 + vite :3001
#   scripts/docs/capture-stack.sh capture  # run the e2e-docs Playwright project
#   scripts/docs/capture-stack.sh stop     # stop the processes (data kept)
#   scripts/docs/capture-stack.sh destroy  # stop + drop the database + the KV mount
set -euo pipefail
ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../.." && pwd)"
RUN="${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/dataq-docs-capture"
mkdir -p "$RUN"
API_PORT="${DOCS_API_PORT:-8001}"
WEB_PORT="${DOCS_WEB_PORT:-3001}"
DB_NAME="${DOCS_DB_NAME:-dataq_docs}"
KV_MOUNT="${DOCS_KV_MOUNT:-docs-capture}"
COMPOSE=(docker compose -f "$ROOT/docker-compose.yml")

_env() {
  set -a
  # shellcheck disable=SC1091
  source "$ROOT/.env"
  set +a
  export DATABASE_URL="postgresql+psycopg2://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@localhost:5432/${DB_NAME}"
  export REDIS_URL="redis://localhost:6379/3"
  export SECRET_STORE=openbao
  export OPENBAO_ADDR="http://localhost:8200"
  export OPENBAO_TOKEN
  export OPENBAO_MOUNT="$KV_MOUNT"
  export AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=true
  # Explicitly NOT OTP: a developer's .env.app may configure it, and OTP wins
  # over dev-bypass at import time (core/auth.py).
  export AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS= AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS= AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST= AUTH_EMAIL_FROM=
  export DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL=
  export ENVIRONMENT=dev
  export REDACTED@dataq.local
  export RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false

export RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false
  export DATAQ_ROLE_TOKENS_PATH="$RUN/.role-tokens.json"
}

_alive() { [ -f "$RUN/$1.pid" ] && kill -0 "$(cat "$RUN/$1.pid")" 2>/dev/null; }

_psql() { "${COMPOSE[@]}" exec -T postgres psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d postgres -tAc "$1"; }

_bao() { curl -sf -X "$1" -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "http://localhost:8200/v1/$2" "${@:3}"; }

start() {
  _env
  if _alive api || _alive web; then
    echo "already running (pids in $RUN) — run 'stop' first"; exit 1
  fi
  _psql "select 1 from pg_database where datname='${DB_NAME}'" | grep -q 1 \
    || _psql "create database ${DB_NAME}" >/dev/null
  _bao GET "sys/mounts/${KV_MOUNT}" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
    || _bao POST "sys/mounts/${KV_MOUNT}" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
         -d '{"type":"kv","options":{"version":"2"}}' >/dev/null
  (cd "$ROOT/backend" && conda run -n dataq --no-capture-output alembic upgrade head >"$RUN/alembic.log" 2>&1)
  (cd "$ROOT" && conda run -n dataq --no-capture-output python -m backend.scripts.seed_dev >"$RUN/seed.log" 2>&1)
  (cd "$ROOT" && nohup conda run -n dataq --no-capture-output \
      uvicorn backend.app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$API_PORT" >"$RUN/api.log" 2>&1 </dev/null & echo $! >"$RUN/api.pid")
  for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
    curl -sf "http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}/api/v1/me" >/dev/null && break; sleep 1
  done
  curl -sf "http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}/api/v1/me" >/dev/null || { echo "api did not come up"; tail -20 "$RUN/api.log"; exit 1; }
  # The seed carries no llm_settings row; the LLM captures need a saved, enabled
  # OpenAI-compatible config so a fresh stack regenerates the same images. The
  # key is a placeholder (Ollama ignores it); Test only shows OK when a server
  # answers at DOCS_LLM_BASE_URL.
  curl -sf -o /dev/null -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    "http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}/api/v1/admin/llm" \
    -d "{\"provider\":\"openai_compatible\",\"model\":\"${DOCS_LLM_MODEL:-qwen2.5:14b}\",\"base_url\":\"${DOCS_LLM_BASE_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1}\",\"api_key\":\"docs-capture-placeholder\",\"structured_output\":\"prompt_json\",\"enabled\":true}" \
    || { echo "could not seed the LLM provider config"; exit 1; }
  # Optional: a real Snowflake reader connection + suite, for the SQL-generation and
  # suggest-checks captures (both need to introspect a live table — a fake config
  # errors on every call). Skipped when DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT is unset, so the base
  # capture set still works with no warehouse credentials at hand; export it (plus
  # DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_USER/_SECRET, the rest default to the harness reader's shape —
  # DATAQ_DB.RETAIL, warehouse DATAQ_WH, role DATAQ_READER) before `start` to enable
  # them. `DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET` is read from the environment only — never logged,
  # never written to a file here.
  if [ -n "${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT:-}" ]; then
    conn_id="$(curl -sf -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      "http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}/api/v1/connections" \
      -d "{\"name\":\"snowflake-docs-reader\",\"type\":\"snowflake\",\"env\":\"dev\",\"config\":{\"account\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT}\",\"user\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_USER:?export DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_USER to enable the live-warehouse captures}\",\"database\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE:-DATAQ_DB}\",\"schema\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_SCHEMA:-RETAIL}\",\"warehouse\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE:-DATAQ_WH}\",\"role\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_ROLE:-DATAQ_READER}\",\"auth_type\":\"password\"},\"secret\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET:?export DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_SECRET to enable the live-warehouse captures}\"}" \
      | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin).get("id",""))')" \
      || { echo "could not create the docs Snowflake connection"; exit 1; }
    if [ -z "$conn_id" ]; then
      echo "docs Snowflake connection created but the response carried no id — aborting rather than silently skipping the live-warehouse captures"; exit 1
    fi
    curl -sf -o /dev/null -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      "http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}/api/v1/suites" \
      -d "{\"name\":\"Retail orders (reader)\",\"connection_id\":\"$conn_id\",\"target\":{\"table\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_TABLE:-ORDERS_HEADER}\",\"schema\":\"${DOCS_SNOWFLAKE_SCHEMA:-RETAIL}\"}}" \
      || { echo "could not create the docs Snowflake suite"; exit 1; }
    echo "live-warehouse captures enabled (connection $conn_id)"
  fi
  (cd "$ROOT/frontend" && VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET="http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}" VITE_AUTH_DEV_BYPASS=true \
      nohup pnpm dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$WEB_PORT" --strictPort >"$RUN/web.log" 2>&1 </dev/null & echo $! >"$RUN/web.pid")
  for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
    curl -sf "http://127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT}/" >/dev/null && break; sleep 1
  done
  curl -sf "http://127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT}/" >/dev/null || { echo "vite did not come up"; tail -20 "$RUN/web.log"; exit 1; }
  echo "docs capture stack up: web http://127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT} api http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT} (logs in $RUN)"
}

capture() {
  (cd "$ROOT/frontend" && E2E_DOCS=1 E2E_DOCS_BASE_URL="http://127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT}" \
      pnpm exec playwright test --project docs-capture "$@")
}

stop() {
  for p in api web; do
    if [ -f "$RUN/$p.pid" ]; then
      pid="$(cat "$RUN/$p.pid")"
      pkill -TERM -P "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
      kill -TERM "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true
      rm -f "$RUN/$p.pid"
    fi
  done
  # Belt and braces for orphans: match the real argv shapes (uvicorn's own
  # process; Vite runs as node …/vite.js --host … --port N).
  pkill -f "uvicorn backend.app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port ${API_PORT}" 2>/dev/null || true
  pkill -f "vite.js --host 127.0.0.1 --port ${WEB_PORT}" 2>/dev/null || true
  echo "stopped"
}

destroy() {
  _env
  stop
  _psql "drop database if exists ${DB_NAME}" >/dev/null && echo "dropped ${DB_NAME}"
  _bao DELETE "sys/mounts/${KV_MOUNT}" >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "removed KV mount ${KV_MOUNT}" || true
  rm -f "$RUN/.role-tokens.json"
}

case "${1:-}" in
  start) start ;;
  capture) shift; capture "$@" ;;
  stop) stop ;;

content.content:
`orders`, three runs build the history. When a load then leaves `customer_email` empty,
the next run reports `customer_email` · `null_pct` · value `100` against a mean of about
`2`, and fails.

**Per-period metrics** watch a value for each calendar day or week instead of the whole
table: `period_row_count` is the rows whose date falls in the period, and `period_sum` is
the sum of a numeric column over them. Use them for a table that only grows, where the
whole-table row count has no "normal" to return to: orders per day, sales amount per week.

- `date_column` says which column dates a row, `period` is `day` or `week` (Monday to
  Sunday), and `period_sum` also names a `value_column`.
- Only **complete** periods are judged. `timezone` (an IANA name spelled exactly, default
  `UTC`) is the zone the date column's values are written in, and decides when a day ends.
  A period is judged once it has been closed for `settle_hours` (default 6), so a suite that
  runs just after midnight does not judge yesterday before the nightly load has landed.
  Raise it for a table that fills in slowly.
- Set `timezone` to the data's zone, not to where you are. If the column holds UTC
  timestamps and `timezone` is `Asia/Tokyo`, a morning run in Tokyo judges a UTC day that
  still has hours to go, and that short count becomes the day's stored point.
- Each period gets **one** stored point, written the first time it is judged. Running the
  suite again the same day measures the period again and reports it, but the baseline keeps
  the first value, and rows that arrive later do not revise it. The result's `recorded` field
  says whether this run stored a point.
- A row is placed by the date the warehouse returns for `date_column`. A timestamp with a
  time zone is read in the warehouse session's zone, which DataQ does not set, so for such a
  column `timezone` only decides when a period counts as complete.
- A period with no rows counts as 0, for the sum as well.
- Changing `date_column`, `period` or `value_column` starts the history again, because the
  earlier points measured something else. Changing `timezone` or `settle_hours` does not.
- **The history is seeded on the first run.** One query reads up to three years of past
  periods from the table's own rows, so the check scores on its first run instead of waiting
  for `min_points` runs. Seeded points are marked `backfilled` and points a run measured are
  `observed`, and that mark never changes: a backfilled point is what the table says today
  about the past, which a restatement or a purge can have altered. Every result's `history`
  says how many of each it was scored against and what seeding came to (`seeding`: `done`,
  `off` or `failed`); the result of the run that seeded also carries `seeded`, with the
  number of points kept and where they start.
- Seeding starts at the period **after** the first one that has rows, because that first
  period is usually partial (a table that began on a Thursday has a four-day first week),
  and counts a later period with no rows as 0.
- It is one scan of the table: set `backfill` to `false` for a warehouse that bills per
  query, or where old rows are archived, and the check starts empty and waits. Switching it
  on later seeds around the points runs have already measured, which are kept.
- If the seeding query fails, the check still runs, starts empty and says so. It tries again
  on the next two runs and then stops; dropping the check's baseline starts over.
- A per-period check keeps three years of periods on top of its window.

**Yearly seasonality** (`yearly: true`, on the per-period metrics) makes a check compare
with the same time in earlier years as well as with its recent window. It is for data with a
yearly rhythm: a sale every November, a quiet week at the end of December.

- The check works out how this time last year compared with the days around it then, and
  expects the same now. If last year's sale day ran at 2.4 times its surroundings, 2.4 times
  the current level is expected this year: arriving near that is normal, and arriving flat (a
  load that failed during the sale) fails.
- A peak gets room in proportion to its size. If an ordinary day varies by 3%, a sale day is
  allowed about 3% of its own, larger, value. With two or three earlier years, how much
  they disagreed about the size of the peak is added to that room.
- The days after a peak are not judged against the peak, because the peak was expected too.
- A day is matched to the same weekday nearest the same date a year back, and a week to the
  week containing that date. With two earlier years the index is their average; with
  three, the middle one.
- It needs a year of history, which seeding supplies at once where the table still holds its
  past. Until a period has an earlier year to compare with, the check scores exactly as it
  does without the setting and the result says why: `yearly.applied` is `false` with a
  `reason`.
- When it is applied, the result's `yearly` gives the `level`, the `index`, the `expected`
  value, the earlier periods it was `matched` to and the `ratios` each of them ran at. The
  result's `mean` and `stddev` are then the centre and spread the run was scored against.
- One earlier year cannot tell a yearly event from a one-off. The check uses it and says how
  many `years` stand behind the comparison. When the years disagree a lot (two had a sale,
  one did not), the comparison is loose, and `ratios` shows why.
- A peak tied to a fixed date (25 December) or one that moves by more than a few days is not
  lined up by this matching.
- Not available for whole-table row count, freshness age or the column profile.

For example, a daily `period_sum` check on `orders.amount` with `yearly` on, created in
October 2025 on a table that holds 2024: on Wednesday 26 November 2025, in the sale, it
expects about 2.4 times the last fortnight's level because Wednesday 27 November 2024 ran at
2.4 times its own. Sales of 240 against a level of 100 pass; sales of 100 fail.

**Declared seasonal periods** line up the peaks the weekday matching cannot: a sale that
moves by more than a few days, or a fixed date such as 25 December. They live in one
workspace calendar, managed through the REST API under `/api/v1/admin/seasonal-periods`
(there is no calendar screen in the app yet; anyone signed in can read it, workspace
admins change it, every change is audited, and AI assistants read it with the
`list_seasonal_periods` MCP tool). An entry
is either **recurring**, a month-and-day range every year that may wrap the year end (20
December to 5 January; a 29 February bound is taken as 28 February in a year without one),
or **dated**, an explicit start and end. Dated entries that share a **series** (compared
case-insensitively) are the occurrences of one period across years: "Spring sale 2025" and
"Spring sale 2026" with series "Spring sale".

An entry changes no check until it is attached: a per-period anomaly check with `yearly` on
lists the entries that apply to its table in `seasonal_periods` (their ids; an unknown id is
refused when the check is saved, and an entry that any check still names cannot be deleted —
the refusal names the checks). While attached:

- A day inside the period is compared with the same offset into the period's **previous
  occurrence** (recurring: the same range the year before, then two and three years back;
  dated: the earlier entries of its series), instead of the nearest weekday. The result's
  `declared.inside` names the entry and the occurrence, and `declared.inside.matched` the
  earlier days it was compared with. A weekly check works in weeks that start on Monday: a
  week is inside a period when its Monday is, and it is matched only to a week that lies
  inside the earlier occurrence on both sides, so a period that began mid-week last year
  may have one week fewer to match.
- Days inside any attached period are left out of the level, so the weeks after a sale are
  not judged against it (`declared.excluded_from_level` counts them), and an ordinary day is
  not matched to an earlier year's sale day.
- **First year.** With no earlier occurrence in the history, the check knows a rise is
  expected but not how large. A value **above** the level is reported as within the declared
  period and not banded (the run reads `skipped`, with `reason: within_declared_period`); a
  value **below** it is judged against the ordinary level as usual, so a load that fails
  during a first-year sale still alerts. `declared.inside.first_year` says when this applied.
- Every result on an attached check also carries `declared.z_score_without`,
  `declared.verdict_without` and `declared.verdict_changed`: what the run would have scored
  with no calendar, so it is always possible to tell whether the calendar changed the
  verdict. An attached id with no entry behind it (which the delete refusal prevents) is
  listed in `declared.missing`; the check keeps running.

A suite export carries the ids; importing it into a workspace whose calendar does not hold
them is refused with the ids named.

**Detected seasonal periods** are what a per-period check's own history shows, read when
someone asks: `GET /api/v1/suites/{suite_id}/checks/{check_id}/seasonal-periods/detected`
(view access to the suite), or the `get_detected_seasonal_periods` MCP tool. A period is
detected where the value ran at **1.5 times** its level or more (taken as scoring takes it: the
median of the window before it with `yearly` on, attached declared periods left out, and the
mean of the window without `yearly`) for at least **two days
in a row**, or one week on a weekly check. A single day is a spike, not a period, and a day
with no point ends a run. Seen at the same time of year in two or more years (within a week
of each other, so a sale that moves a few days still matches) it is **recurring**; in one
year, **seen once**. The response lists each period's occurrences by year, with their peak
ratio and how many of their points were seeded from the table rather than seen by a run, the
month-and-day span a recurring one covers, any attached entry that overlaps it, and how much
history stood behind it (points, first and last day, years).

A detected period is a description. It is not stored and **changes no verdict**: only an
entry on the calendar, attached to the check, does. An empty list says less than it seems:
`reason` is set when nothing could be looked at (`not_a_per_period_metric`, `no_history`,
`insufficient_history`, `invalid_config`); with no reason, the history was read and nothing
reached 1.5 times for long enough (or the stored history was discarded because the
check's metric, date column or day/week setting was edited). A peak that lasts more than
about half the check's window of prior periods (same-weekday periods when seasonality is
on) lifts the level with it, so its occurrence is reported shorter than it ran; attaching
a calendar entry over it fixes that, for detection as for scoring.

A workspace admin turns a detected period into a calendar entry with
`POST /api/v1/admin/seasonal-periods/promote`, naming the check, the period's `start` (its
most recent occurrence, as the detection returned it) and a `name`. The history is read
again, so a period it no longer shows is refused, and so is a season an entry on the
calendar already covers (the refusal names the entry to attach instead). A recurring period becomes a recurring
entry over the month-and-day span; one seen once becomes a dated entry, optionally in a
`series`. With `attach: true` the check names the new entry too, in the same change, so a
check that cannot take it (one without `yearly`) leaves no entry behind. The new entry is
audited as created, with the period it came from.

### Comparison check (all datasources — ADR 0015)

*Does this dataset reconcile against that one?* A comparison check diffs the suite's
dataset (the **target under test**) against a **baseline** on any other datasource
connection — cross-type and cross-env both work (Snowflake DEV vs Snowflake QA, or
Snowflake vs the flat-file extract it was loaded from). Rows are joined on the key
columns you pick, producing **matched / mismatched / additional-per-side** buckets
with a mismatch-% metric that bands through the normal severity thresholds. Reads
are capped fail-fast (`COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS`), samples are redacted like every other

# Admin control centre

The admin area is where a **workspace Admin** sees the whole workspace and manages the
things that are shared rather than owned: membership, roles, access grants, workspace
settings, compliance evidence, and inbound integrations.

It lives at `/admin` and is split into six deep-linkable sub-pages. The tab you are on
**is** the URL, so any tab can be bookmarked, shared with another admin, or reloaded
without losing your place. `/admin` on its own lands on **Overview**.

## Page map

| Tab | URL | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Overview | `/admin/overview` | Workspace counts — members, suites, open incidents, runs today — plus a "needs attention" feed and a workspace-health checklist, each row linking to the thing that needs fixing. |
| Members | `/admin/members` | Every user with their workspace role (editable in place) and every per-suite access grant. |
| Suites | `/admin/suites` | Every suite in the workspace, unscoped by sharing: owner, datasource, environment, check count, share count. |
| Settings | `/admin/settings` | Workspace facts and the sign-in method, the email pre-flight test, reusable notification channels, the LLM provider, zero-sample mode, the health-score weights, the secret-store notice, and the danger zone. |
| Compliance | `/admin/compliance` | The audit log with its filters and retention disclosure, audit-chain verification, the data-subject-rights tools, and the deployment / data-residency posture. |
| Integrations | `/admin/integrations` | Ready-to-paste inbound webhook URLs for each configured orchestration provider, with the auth mode each one uses. |

The former standalone **Settings** page has moved here: `/settings` now redirects to
`/admin/settings`, and the sidebar carries a single **Admin** entry rather than two links
to the same area.

## Who can open it

Every admin route is gated **at the route**, not by hiding a button. A user who is not a
workspace Admin gets the Forbidden page — including on a direct deep link to a sub-page or
to `/settings`, and including after a demotion, since the role is resolved per request.
No admin data is fetched for them at all.

Admin is one of two authorization axes; see the
[features overview](features.md) for how workspace roles compose with per-suite sharing.

## What loads when

Each sub-page owns its own data. Opening **Compliance** fetches the audit log and the
posture and nothing else; the members and suites tables are not read until you open their
tab. Switching tabs is a navigation, so the page you leave stops holding data you are no
longer looking at.

## Overview

`/admin/overview` is the workspace's morning page: four counts, everything that currently
needs attention, and a checklist of the health signals themselves.

### The stat cards

| Card | The number | The line under it |
|---|---|---|
| Members | Every user row in the workspace. | How many were admitted but have not signed in yet — see below. |
| Suites | Every suite, unscoped by sharing. | How many **distinct connections** those suites target; a connection no suite uses is not counted. |
| Open incidents | Every unresolved incident. | How many of those have been acknowledged. Acknowledging silences nothing, so an acknowledged incident is still open and still counted. |
| Runs today | Runs created since the start of the current **UTC** day (not your local day). | Succeeded, failed and running. Queued and cancelled runs are in the total but not in those three, so they need not add up. |

**Members: "pending first sign-in is not tracked yet."** A user row is created *by* a first
successful sign-in, so someone admitted at the identity provider who has never signed in
leaves no trace in DataQ at all. The card says the number is untracked rather than showing
a `0` that would claim everybody admitted has arrived.

If a card cannot be loaded it shows an em dash and the failure, never a zero.

### Needs attention

One row per thing that is wrong or unknown, each with a verb that takes you to where it is
fixed — the connection, the suites list, or the health item further down the page.

| Row | What raised it |
|---|---|
| Polling stalled / failing | An orchestration connection is overdue for a poll, or is being polled on schedule and erroring. Pipeline completions may not be reaching DataQ. |
| Stored credential rejected | A datasource rejected the stored credential the last time real work used it. |
| Trigger env mismatch | A pipeline keeps succeeding in one environment while the only enabled binding targets another, so no suite is triggered. Only mismatches on suites you can see are listed. |
| Orphan secrets found | The last sweep found stored credentials that no connection references any more. |
| Anything marked **not monitored** | See below. |

An empty feed means nothing is wrong **among the signals listed in the health checklist**.
Anything not in that checklist is unmonitored, not clear.

# changelog.d — one file per change

Every PR that changes something a user, deployer or API client would notice adds **one
small file here** instead of editing `docs/site/reference/changelog.md`. The published
page renders these under **Unreleased** at build time; at release
`scripts/changelog.py assemble` moves them into a dated section and deletes them.

## Filename

```
<number>.<section>.md         e.g. 2395.changed.md
<number>-<n>.<section>.md     a second entry for the same number, e.g. 2440-2.added.md
```

- `<number>` — the issue the change belongs to (the PR number if there is no issue).
- `<n>` — `2`, `3`, … for further fragments of the same number.
- `<section>` — `breaking` | `security` | `added` | `changed` | `fixed`.

Only files matching this grammar (plus this README) may live here.

## Body

The bullet's text in Markdown, **without** the leading `- `, continuation lines unindented.
Lead with a bold phrase, as the existing entries do, and describe the behaviour — never cite
an issue or PR number, the page is public (CONTRIBUTING rule 41).

```markdown
**Changelog entries are collected one file per change.** A PR adds a fragment under
`changelog.d/` and the published page assembles them, so two PRs never conflict on the
changelog.
2440-2.added.md
2440-3.added.md
2440-4.added.md
2440.added.md

content.content:
**A declared seasonal calendar for anomaly checks.** Workspace admins keep one calendar of named seasonal periods (recurring month-and-day ranges, or dated entries grouped into a series across years) through the REST API, audited like other admin changes. A per-period anomaly check with `yearly` on attaches the entries that apply to its table: a day inside one is compared with the same day of the period's previous occurrence, so a sale that moves or a fixed date lines up, and the days after it are not judged against it. In a period's first year a rise is reported as within the period rather than banded, while a drop still alerts. Every result says which entry applied and what the run would have scored without the calendar.
**Detected seasonal periods, and promoting one to the calendar.** A per-period anomaly check now reports the seasonal periods its own history shows: runs of at least two days (or one week) at 1.5 times the level the check is scored against, called recurring when they come at the same time in two or more years and seen once otherwise, with each year's dates, peak ratio and how much history stood behind them. A detected period is a description and changes no verdict. A workspace admin can promote one to the declared calendar (a recurring period as a month-and-day range, one seen once as a dated entry) and attach it to the check in the same step. AI assistants gain two read-only MCP tools, `list_seasonal_periods` and `get_detected_seasonal_periods`.

## Summary

- Phase 6 of ADR 0048: the seasonal calendar, the per-period editor fields and the trend in the app. **Admin → Calendar** (`/admin/calendar`, a new admin tab, route-gated to Admins like the rest of the area) lists, adds, edits and deletes calendar entries (every year on the same dates, or on specific dates with a series, plus a note). A refused delete lists the checks that still attach the entry, each linking to its editor.
- **Check editor**: the per-period date and sum columns suggest the target's columns (read once, on first focus), the time zone is picked from the browser's IANA list, and **Declared seasonal periods** is a multi-select of calendar entries by name and dates, shown only with **Yearly seasonality** on. With yearly off it says what to do; on a check that already has entries attached it warns that saving removes them (the backend refuses attachments without yearly, so they cannot be kept). Members see the entries; only Admins get the link to manage them. No new boolean field: the editor sends nothing new for a check that never used the calendar (tested), so existing checks do not change by being opened and saved.
- **Trend** of a per-period anomaly check: for each period a run judged, the band it was scored against (its centre ± k × spread) and, where the yearly comparison applied, the expected value as its own dashed line; seeded points are hollow, observed ones filled; attached calendar entries are shaded with their names; detected periods (from the detected endpoint) are outlined and listed under the chart with **Promote to calendar** for Admins (name, series for a seen-once period, note, and "also attach", which is disabled with the reason when the check has no yearly). The caption now says what the band is and, per reason, on how many shown periods the yearly comparison did not apply; the old caption that called a yearly band "the recent window only" is gone. The Table view carries the same numbers per period (scored against, expected or why not, declared period). After a promote that attaches, an open editor re-reads the check so a later save does not undo the attach.
- **Run detail**: each per-period anomaly result has a compact "How this period was judged": the period, the expected value (level × index, years) or why yearly did not apply, the band and z, the declared entry and occurrence (first year / not banded), whether the calendar changed the verdict and what it would have been, missing entries, and how much of the history was seeded.
- **Backend (read model only)**: `GET …/checks/{id}/history` points gain an optional `seasonal` object read from the stored result payload (period start, mean, stddev, yearly applied/reason, expected, declared entry name, banded, verdict_changed). It is the same sensitivity class as `metric_value`, which the endpoint already returns; non-per-period results get `null`. `openapi.json` and the generated client regenerated (pinned ruff 0.16.5).
- Network idle: every new fetch is one-shot on mount (history, baseline, detected, calendar) or on first focus (columns); nothing polls.

I reviewed PR #2492 (`feature/seasonal-calendar-ui`, head `6a7be254`) at high effort and found 10 issues. All 10 are posted as inline comments on the PR, each linked in the list below. I did not run the PR, so these are unverified candidates. Two of them, the band centre and the 180-result window, I checked against the backend code (`seasonal.py`, `anomaly.py`).

```json
[
  {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/CheckTrend.tsx","line":585,"summary":"The caption says the yearly band is centred on the expected value (the dashed line), but the backend centres it elsewhere, so the chart's band and dashed line disagree.","failure_scenario":"seasonal.History.score sets centre = expected + fmean(distances)*scale, and anomaly.py writes that centre into observed_value.mean. The chart draws the band at j.mean ± k·stddev and the dashed line at j.expected, so the band sits off the line whenever the mean distance is not zero. The SeasonalPointRead and SeasonalPoint docs repeat the claim."},
  {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/SeasonalTrend.tsx","line":99,"summary":"Declared and detected periods are snapped to plotted period starts, so on weekly or monthly checks, or for one-period occurrences, the highlight is missing or zero width.","failure_scenario":"A weekly check with Black Friday attached as Thu 26 – Sun 29 Nov has no Monday inside the range, so snapToDays returns null and nothing is drawn. A range holding one period start gives x1 === x2, a 0-px ReferenceArea. The caption still says 'Highlighted: … (Black Friday)'."},
  {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/SeasonalTrend.tsx","line":158,"summary":"The band Area and the dashed Expected Line use connectNulls={false} with no dots, so a judged period with no judged neighbour draws nothing.","failure_scenario":"With seeded history and only the newest period judged, both the range Area and the dot-less Line have one point between nulls and render nothing. The caption still reports '(1 shown) … applied (1 of 1) … the dashed line'."},
  {"file":"frontend/src/pages/CheckEdit.tsx","line":382,"summary":"onCheckChanged={onRestored} reloads the check after promote-and-attach, and the [check] effect's setFieldsValue then wipes the user's unsaved edits.","failure_scenario":"The user edits thresholds, opens the trend drawer and promotes with 'Also attach'. The form re-seeds from the server and the unsaved edits are lost. Not re-seeding would instead detach the entry on save, because config is PATCHed wholesale. The merge should touch config.seasonal_periods only."},
  {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/CheckTrend.tsx","line":248,"summary":"A per-period check fetches the last 180 results, not 180 periods, so a check that runs more often than its period gets bands on only a few periods.","failure_scenario":"An hourly run on a daily period: 180 results cover about 7.5 days, so only about 8 of up to 180 plotted periods get a band or expected value, and 'N shown' undercounts."},
  {"file":"backend/app/services/check_service.py","line":1890,"summary":"The history query loads the full observed_value JSONB for every check type to read a few keys that only per-period anomaly results have.","failure_scenario":"For comparison, schema_drift and column-profile checks it pulls 180 large blobs per trend request, and RunDetail mounts a trend per expanded row.   {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/CheckTrend.tsx","line":577,"summary":"A failed baseline fetch is swallowed to null, and the caption then states 'No shown period has a result yet' even when the history holds judged results.","failure_scenario":"A transient 5xx on getCheckBaseline leaves observations empty, so the caption makes a wrong statement instead of saying the overlay is unavailable."},

  {"file":"frontend/src/components/checks/SeasonalTrend.tsx","line":206,"summary":"Detection reasons invalid_config and not_a_per_period_metric fall through to 'none — no run of periods … in 0 stored points'.","failure_scenario":"When detection never ran because the config failed to parse, the UI reads as if it ran and found no seasonality."},

import subprocess
